newsitem.title: USA: NASA finds crack in shuttle launch platform.
newsitem.headline: NASA finds crack in shuttle launch platform.

text.p: The space shuttle Discovery's journey to its Florida launch pad was halted for four hours on Friday after a large crack appeared in the spaceship's launch platform, NASA officials said.
The shuttle was being moved in readiness for a scheduled Feb. 11 blastoff on NASA's second mission to service the Hubble Space Telescope.
The rollout was halted when a loud bang was heard and a 24-foot-long (7.3 metres) crack appeared in the deck of the launch platform, said NASA spokeswoman Lisa Malone.
Several doors within the two-story steel structure were found to be jammed after the incident, which occurred just a short distance from the shuttle's assembly building.
Structural engineers determined it was safe to complete the shuttle's move to the launch pad but planned to make additional inspections to see if the platform would be safe for the launch.
"We're not out of the woods yet," Malone said.

The Y-shaped crack occurred in the 0.5-0.75 inch-thick (1.3-1.9 cm) steel plate on the surface of the platform, which was built in the 1960s for the Apollo moon programme and modified for use by the shuttle.
Cold weather at the Florida launch pad may have played a part in the damage, said Malone. The temperature was 39 degrees Fahrenheit (3.8 degrees Celsius) as the shuttle was being moved.
The structure, which weighs 11 million pounds (5 million kg) with the shuttle attached, is rolled out to the launch pad atop a tracked transporter that inches forward at just 1 mph (1.6 kph).

Discovery is being prepared for a critical mission to service the Hubble Space Telescope. During the 11-day flight the shuttle crew will install in Hubble two new scientific instruments and replace worn out equipment.
Meanwhile, in orbit, the crew of the space shuttle Atlantis and the Mir space station continued their joint work.
Almost three tons of gear was being moved between the two craft to resupply the Russian space station and return experiment results to Earth.
